title: Comparing Any Two Fractions
short: Rename with a common denominator or numerator, then compare.
trouble: Children compare only the numerators or only the denominators of unlike fractions.

blocks.html: When benchmarks do not settle it, make the fractions easy to compare. You know how to make equivalent fractions, so rename them with the same denominator (or the same numerator).

To compare $\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{3}{5}$, rename both with a common denominator, such as 15: $\dfrac{10}{15}$ and $\dfrac{9}{15}$. Now the pieces are the same size, so the one with more pieces is greater: $\dfrac{2}{3} > \dfrac{3}{5}$. Both fractions must refer to the same whole.
Comparing thirds with fifths is like comparing 2 large slices with 3 small slices. Cutting both into fifteenths makes all the slices the same size; then you only count.

blocks.title: One denominator is a multiple of the other

blocks.html: Comparing only the numerators ("3 is more than 2, so $\dfrac{3}{5}$ is bigger") or only the denominators. Unlike pieces cannot be counted against each other. Rename first, then compare.
